SIU Mpumalanga Land fraud

By: Bernadette Maguire | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Special Investigations Unit is meant to be a crack unit clamping down on corruption in South Africa - but critics say they're toothless bulldogs throwing good money after bad.

Summary:
In 2010 a scam was exposed in Mpumalanga involving top officials buying land for low cost housing developments. High profile individuals linked to the ANC who were involved in spatial planning then sold the land to municipalities at hugely inflated rates - in one case they paid 16 million and sold it to the Nelspruit municipality for 37 million - 21 million was pocketed through a network of companies by politically linked individuals. Some of this money also went back into ANC coffers according to an SIU Whistleblower. A report was commissioned by the SIU, they concluded a report that fingered these individuals and they were ready to effect arrests. But that's when the investigation was put on hold and no-one ever held to account. It's the story of countless other SIU investigations - as soon as they uncover corruption linked to politically connected individuals the investigation is stalled...indefinitely.

Further information:
This comes at great cost - these investigations cost around 4 million rand each and yet no money is recovered from the guilty parties.

Shocking against a backdrop of 700 billion lost to corruption over the past 20 years. Thats the equivalent of 7 Medupi power stations...and equates to a million rand stolen every day over the past 20 years.

We ask why so few arrests, why so few successes? Why is the SIU not acting on its mandate and why so many sacred cows?

Can South Africa afford this?

Extra Budget Items:
given the distances we will need to travel to Nelspruit so at the very least we will need an additional travel day.

Press Release:


Mpumalanga Land Deals
Why was R50m of tax payers’ money used to buy a farm worth R4.8m? And why was R37.5m spent on another, worth just R17.5m? Millions have allegedly been siphoned off in an Mpumalanga project meant to benefit the poor. Four years after the alleged land scam was exposed, one of the farms lies deserted and others are home to squatters with no water and no electricity. Carte Blanche asks: why has the SIU’s investigation run cold?


Script:


Script SIU


VO: 22”

Everyone wants to make a fast buck. In Mpumalanga land deals have provided a quick fix. In 2011 an alleged land scandal was exposed.

- This 74 ha farm Naauwpoort farm in Emahlaleni was sold for 37.5 and a half million – BUT only 17,5 million was received by the seller. In fact, middle men pocketed 20 million for so-called professional fees

- Rietspruit farm in Ermelo - bought for 11.9 million and sold for 36 million. BUT astonishingly these transactions were processed on the same day (slower)

- And Festina Lente farm in Malelane officially valued at 4.8 million bought at a grossly inflated 41 million and re-sold for nearly 10 times its original value at 50 million on the same day

Mpumalanga Opposition leader, Anthony Benadie, says around 350 million rands has been spent in this way.

Anthony:
There is well connected individuals buying land from private individuals and selling it off to government to make large sums of profit through the transfer of this land in a very short space of time.

VO:
Leaked reports from a whistleblower show
the flow of money from the department of human settlements to conveyancers and then to middlemen who in most cases resold the properties to local municipalities at these inflated prices – ostensibly to provide housing for the poor.

Anthony:
The land was sold off to government and the project has basically been in standstill since then.

FIX!!!!
Were to be residential developments…. VO: 5”
Armed with the reports we went on a road trip to check for ourselves. First we headed out to Naauwpoort farm in Emahlaleni. Nothing could have prepared us for the apocalyptic settlement that greeted us.

Bongani link
You know, I came here looking for a farm, I thought there would be a farmhouse, some kind of sign that there was once livestock or crops here, instead its one of the most bleak environments I have ever seen and even if you were to accept that a residential development was meant to be built here – its in the shadow of a power station!

VO:
Thousands of people have settled in makeshift shacks in the hope of getting a house here. Grandmother Elizabeth Makgale is one of them. 4 years on she says they’re still waiting for electricity and water. The people here say all they get are empty promises.

Siphiso:
We just saw people here to register us. They promised us that they would build us houses. We gave them our ID’s and they registered us. We never got a report back, nothing was done.

VO: 3”
Many of the residents have lost hope.

White
The most popular thing here is that children quit school at a very young age, there’s no future here for them.

VO:
The department of human settlements originally put up the money in order to build new townships. Then they paid it into a Nelspruit attorneys trust account. The attorney, Mduduzi Singwane then paid the seller, the estate agents and the lion’s share was siphoned off to various middle men.

One of the middle men was a company called Little River Trading – the directors included Patrick Chirwa, Harrington Dhlamini and Robert Burwise –

these men also also ran a town planning firm Sisonke development Planners. Chirwa and Dlamini are former co-directors in a company with Premier David Mabuza. These political linkages are key says this whistleblower.

Bongani:
How much is the fact that a number of the individuals concerned with these transactions are politically influential people?

SIU whistleblower:
Well most of them are.

Bongani:
Would that be a factor?

Whistleblower:
Well it tends to be…

VO
So we called alleged middleman Harrington Dlamini.

Phone call
Bongani:
There are allegations against you as a director of Little River Trading…

Dhlamini: Yebo

Bongani: That you unduly benefitted from an illegtal transaction….

Dhlamini: Yes

Bongani: For the purchase of a farm….


Dhlamini: Ja

VO: 6
He offered his version on why his company earned the 20 million middle man fee for the Naauwpoort farm.

Dlamini:
Thereafter with our money we hired an airplane. We hired someone who is going to do what is known as aerial photography. With our money we hired a land surveyor, with our money we did all these processes. Including the lawyers to make the land a township. As we speak now the land is an approved township.

VO:
Looking at Naauwpoort it was hard to believe that any thought had gone into developing a township there - it appears this only happened on paper.

Whistleblower:
Most of these farm deals were sold as developed townships. Now there are a few complications with that. If it’s a developed township it must be proclaimed, it must form part of the demarcation of the town, there must be town planning, the surveyor general must approve it, when you go back to see how the money flowed it was completely different.

VO: 7”
Astonishingly some of the residents told us that despite the millions spent to buy the land they’re now going to be moved.

Elizabeth:
The premier arrived and said there is nothing they can do for us.

Bongani:
What’s the point of buying land for residential development if you’re going to move the people, that contradicts the very reason for the transaction?

Anthony:
Most of these transactions, as I said, its just about doing the deal, actually. They are characterized by very poor planning processes, very poor research that’s been done and very often we find land that has been acquired for housing or for infrastructure development actually isn’t suitable to do so.

VO: 12”
So we approached conveyancing attorney Mduduzi Singwane who had been involved in all deals. As luck would have it his car pulled in as we arrived.

Bongani: There he is – arriving - Mr Singwane….

VO:
We followed as the AMG floated in but it was his driver who emerged. He pointed us in the direction of his office. After a brief discussion Singwane agreed to speak to us.

Bongani: Specifically around the Naauwpoort farm, its alleged that you claimed to have paid the original owner 37 and a half million rand?

Singwane: That is a subject to an investigation by police.

Bongani: Did you?

Singwane: Police are investigating this matter. Most of the documentary evidence when the transactions started up to the end its with them.

VO: 19”
Singwane was also the conveyancer in another land deal in the town of Ermelo. 4 years on, the Rietspruit farm is virtually deserted except for a handful of squatters eeking out a desperate living there. Farmer Bernard Scheepers met us there.

Bongani: Is this the best deal you have ever seen?

Bernard: By far, I mean in our area, the commercial property value for farmland is ten thousand…

Bongani: Per hectare?

Bernard: Per hectare. This farm isn’t zoned anything else, its farm property, it isn’t zoned for commercial property. It was sold for thirty thousand rand per hectare, which gives you 12 million rand for the whole deal, it was transferred to the municipality for 36 million which gave that guy a 24 million profit.

VO: 3”
He runs a commercial farm next door.

Bernard:
My farm on the other side is a commercial property which has got feedlots, grain storage bins, loading bays, it’s a whole commercial property, its been valued three weeks ago for R18000 per hectare by a credit valuator, this farm sold for R90000 per hectare five years ago with nothing on it.

VO: 5”
We asked the conveyancer about these incredibly swift transfers – some of them done virtually simultanously.

Singwane:
With land restitution matters it takes depending on the request from the Minister, because it’s a sister company, land affairs and the other one, it can take a day, it can take two days, three days.


VO: 20”
On we drove to Malelane. The only improvement on the 70 hectare Festina Lente farm is this dirt road. Local councillor Mariette Preddy says the decision was short sighted. She says the local infrastructure would never cope with an additional 70 hectare housing development. As proof she showed us cellphone footage of the overburdened sewerage system.

Mariette:
There is more than 26 places where the sewerage, that’s from people’s houses, yards and streets and manholes. Water is actually running into the same place where they are actually taking the drinking water out.

VO:
In Ermelo and Malelane the major beneficiary was a closed corporation called Bongiveli run by Pastor Bongani Sibiya and his business partner Vusi Magagula. Again Singwane was the conveyancer.

Bongani: You’re alleged that you are part of a ring with officials in the Human Settlements Department, the Deeds office and that that’s how these matters get through?

Singwane: No that is a baseless allegation. But as far as it goes to a an extent of a ring, its an issue that can be determined by a court of laws. (sic)

shorter
VO: 19”
In fact the matter should have been in a court given that police cases were registered in 2012 and 2013. Instead nothing’s happened.
So we approached the Department of human settlements who provided the money for the deals.

Shorten link VO:
They won’t speak to us and they say the matter is sub-judice.


Film reports VO: 30”
This was of course technically untrue given that the matter is not before a court. Local investigative journalist Tom Nkosi says the province of untouchables.

Tom:
You can do crime there and survive. The unfortunate thing is that these are crimes which are done by the authorities.


Longer


David dube visual … longer VO: 12”
So far only the Head of Department of Human Settlements David Dube was sacked when the scandal broke but was then given a new position as the deputy speaker in the legislature. Political Scientist Dr Mcebisi Ndlentyana says this is a disturbing trend.

Dr Ndletyana:
If you are implicated in something, what should naturally follow is an investigation of sorts. And whoever is suspected of doing something must go to court at least, not be rewarded with a senior position as it seems to have happened in this case.

Tom:
I don’t know how many cases we have seen collapse in this province that are related to corruption and what does this do – it encourages even further corruption.

Antony:
It really is of huge concern that corruption of this nature can take place on such a large scale. Despite the SIU themselves investigating this matter nothing has come of it, its obviously being blocked somewhere by someone.

VO:
So we approached Acting Special investigations unit head Advocate Gerhard Visagie.

Bongani:
How is it that years later some of those processes have not been followed through.

Gerhard:
I really have no answer to that question…that frustration by the public is fully understood.

Bongani:
Do you share that concern?

Gerhard:
In some cases I do yes. Justice delayed is justice denied.

Bongani link:
It goes without saying that maladministration and corruption on this scale takes some planning and co-ordination, a type of crime really, what some are calling the criminalization of the state.

Ntletyana:
Politicians have to demonstrate to us as citizens that they are a lot more serious about fighting corruption. We haven’t been seeing that.

Bongani:
Does that mean our system of accountability failing?

Ntelyana:
To some degree it is failing, the institutions are well established, we have laws, best developed laws, but the challenge is the enforcement of those laws.

VO: 8”
Advocate Visagie who also sits on the executive of the Anti corruption task team assures us there’s action on the cards.

Gerhard:
I can tell you that the investigation is not dead, the decision whether to prosecute or not rests with the NPA but it is my understanding that such a decision will follow in due course.


Tom:
We can only hope that even within these other institutions we will have people who will be dictated to by their own conscience. We must not let these things be forgotten.


10 sec Promo 1:

VO: 6”
4 years after an alleged massive land scam is exposed we ask why has the investigation run cold?

Tom:
Mpumalanga province is like the Mexico of South Africa.

15 sec Promo 2:

VO:
Millions siphoned off in an alleged land scam meant to benefit the poor in Mpumalanga.

Anthony:
The intention is to make

VO:
But why has no-one been brought to book?

15 sec Promo 3:

VO: 12
We go on a road trip to visit farms bought at inflated prices in an alleged land scam - 4 years later one is deserted, and the others are home to squatters with no water and no electricity.

Elizabeth:
It’s very hard here…


VO 15
It appears this investigation into an alleged land scam has run cold. There is a track record of this happening with high profile corruption cases. Take the SIU investigation into Nkandla – there the blame was diverted to the door of the architect.

Mcebisi:
Obviously it focused our attention…not a good job.

VO: 10”
And then there was the BOSASA investigation which has been running for 6 years and still there are no prosecutions. We asked the SIU acting head Advocate Gerhard Visagie why.

Gerhard:
After the completion of the BOSASA investigation to the NPA…it is a priority case.

Tom: I don’t know how many cases we have seen collapse in this province that are related to corruption and what does this do – it encourages even further corruption. Antony: It really is of huge concern that corruption of this nature can take place on such a large scale. Despite the SIU themselves investigating this matter nothing has come of it, its obviously being blocked somewhere by someone. VO: So we approached Acting Special investigations unit head Advocate Gerhard Visagie. Bongani: How is it that years later some of those processes have not been followed through. Gerhard: I really have no answer to that question…that frustration by the public is fully understood. Bongani: Do you share that concern? Gerhard: In some cases I do yes. Justice delayed is justice denied. Bongani link: It goes without saying that maladministration and corruption on this scale takes some planning and co-ordination, a type of crime really, what some are calling the criminalization of the state. Ntletyana: Politicians have to demonstrate to us as citizens that they are a lot more serious about fighting corruption. We haven’t been seeing that. Bongani: Does that mean our system of accountability failing? Ntelyana: To some degree it is failing, the institutions are well established, we have laws, best developed laws, but the challenge is the enforcement of those laws. VO: 8” Advocate Visagie who also sits on the executive of the Anti corruption task team assures us there’s action on the cards. Gerhard: I can tell you that the investigation is not dead, the decision whether to prosecute or not rests with the NPA but it is my understanding that such a decision will follow in due course. Tom: We can only hope that even within these other institutions we will have people who will be dictated to by their own conscience. We must not let these things be forgotten. 10 sec Promo 1: VO: 6” 4 years after an alleged massive land scam is exposed we ask why has the investigation run cold? Tom: Mpumalanga province is like the Mexico of South Africa. 15 sec Promo 2: VO: Millions siphoned off in an alleged land scam meant to benefit the poor in Mpumalanga. Anthony: The intention is to make VO: But why has no-one been brought to book? 15 sec Promo 3: VO: 12 We go on a road trip to visit farms bought at inflated prices in an alleged land scam - 4 years later one is deserted, and the others are home to squatters with no water and no electricity. Elizabeth: It’s very hard here… VO 15 It appears this investigation into an alleged land scam has run cold. There is a track record of this happening with high profile corruption cases. Take the SIU investigation into Nkandla – there the blame was diverted to the door of the architect. Mcebisi: Obviously it focused our attention…not a good job. VO: 10” And then there was the BOSASA investigation which has been running for 6 years and still there are no prosecutions. We asked the SIU acting head Advocate Gerhard Visagie why. Gerhard: After the completion of the BOSASA investigation to the NPA…it is a priority case.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The Special Investigations Unit is meant to be a crack unit clamping down on corruption in South Africa - but critics say they're toothless bulldogs throwing good money after bad.
metadata.Summary: In 2010 a scam was exposed in Mpumalanga involving top officials buying land for low cost housing developments. High profile individuals linked to the ANC who were involved in spatial planning then sold the land to municipalities at hugely inflated rates - in one case they paid 16 million and sold it to the Nelspruit municipality for 37 million - 21 million was pocketed through a network of companies by politically linked individuals. Some of this money also went back into ANC coffers according to an SIU Whistleblower. A report was commissioned by the SIU, they concluded a report that fingered these individuals and they were ready to effect arrests. But that's when the investigation was put on hold and no-one ever held to account. It's the story of countless other SIU investigations - as soon as they uncover corruption linked to politically connected individuals the investigation is stalled...indefinitely.
metadata.Further information: This comes at great cost - these investigations cost around 4 million rand each and yet no money is recovered from the guilty parties. Shocking against a backdrop of 700 billion lost to corruption over the past 20 years. Thats the equivalent of 7 Medupi power stations...and equates to a million rand stolen every day over the past 20 years. We ask why so few arrests, why so few successes? Why is the SIU not acting on its mandate and why so many sacred cows? Can South Africa afford this?
